chapters.title: Chapter 3: Cointegration — Testing Whether a Pair Really Mean-Reverts

lessons.title: Stationarity Explained: Random Walks vs Mean-Reverting Series

children.text: Lesson 1 defined cointegration as the spread between two stocks being stationary. Before that definition is useful, you need a clear picture of what stationary actually means, and just as importantly, what it looks like when a series is not stationary. This lesson builds that picture, since the formal test in Lesson 3 is really just a rigorous way of answering the question this lesson makes visual and intuitive.

body.text: A stationary series has a stable mean it keeps returning to, and shocks to it fade over time. A non-stationary series, like a random walk, has no fixed anchor: shocks are permanent, it can wander any distance in either direction, and its variance keeps growing the longer you watch it. A tradeable spread must behave like the first kind, not the second.

children.text: The Random Walk: No Anchor at All

A random walk is a series where each new value is simply the previous value plus a random shock, with no pull back toward any particular level. Individual stock prices are usually treated as close to a random walk: today's closing price is roughly yesterday's price plus an unpredictable move, which is exactly why nobody can reliably predict tomorrow's price level from today's. This is also why Chapter 1 computed correlation on returns rather than raw prices. A stock's price series is generally non-stationary, wandering without a fixed level, while its day-to-day percentage change (the return) behaves much more like a stationary series, hovering around some average with a roughly stable spread of outcomes.

body.caption: A random walk has no pull toward a fixed level. A mean-reverting series is pulled back toward μ, its long-run mean, with strength controlled by φ.

body.title: Illustrative random walk sample path (simulated, not a real stock)

body.text: This path has no tendency to return to 0, or to any other fixed level. It simply accumulates random shocks. A different simulation of the same random walk process could easily have drifted downward instead, or sideways, or in some other direction entirely. There is no "correct" level this series is trying to get back to, which is exactly what makes it non-stationary.

children.text: The Mean-Reverting Series: A Fixed Anchor

A stationary, mean-reverting series behaves differently. It has a genuine long-run average, and whenever a shock pushes it away from that average, there is a persistent pull back toward it. The series can still wander for a while, a shock does not vanish instantly, but the pull is always there, and the amount by which the series has ever wandered stays bounded over time instead of growing without limit.

body.text: This path oscillates repeatedly between roughly −2 and +2, always pulled back toward an average near 0. This is exactly the behavior a pairs trade depends on: a spread that keeps returning to its historical mean, giving a z-score of −2 or +2 real predictive meaning, since the series has actually visited those levels before and reverted each time.

children.text: The Genuinely Surprising Part of Cointegration

Individual stock prices, as noted above, are generally non-stationary, closer to the random walk chart than the mean-reverting one. HDFC Bank's price on its own is not mean-reverting. Neither is ICICI Bank's. If both legs of a pair are individually non-stationary, how can their spread ever be stationary? This is the actual mathematical content of cointegration: two non-stationary series can still have a specific linear combination, found using the right hedge ratio, that is stationary, even though neither series is stationary on its own. A useful mental picture is two people, each wandering unpredictably on their own, but connected by a leash. Either one alone can end up almost anywhere over time. The distance between them, however, stays bounded, because the leash keeps pulling them back together whenever they drift too far apart. Cointegration is a statistical test for whether that leash actually exists between two stocks, or whether they are just two independent wanderers who happened to look connected for a while.

body.text: Correlation, from Lesson 1, cannot detect the leash directly, because it is measured on returns, not on the wandering distance between the two price levels. A high correlation tells you the two tend to move in the same direction on the same days. It does not tell you whether a leash actually exists holding their price levels together over the long run. Lesson 3 introduces the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test, the standard tool for checking whether a series, including a spread, is stationary.

body.title: Reading the two charts
body.question: Which property distinguishes the mean-reverting sample path from the random walk sample path in this lesson?
options: The mean-reverting path only ever moves in small steps, while the random walk takes large steps
The mean-reverting path is pulled back toward a stable average, while the random walk has no fixed level and can wander indefinitely
The random walk path always trends upward, while the mean-reverting path always trends downward
There is no meaningful difference, both are equally suitable for building a z-score
body.explanation: The defining difference is the presence or absence of a pull back toward a stable average. The mean-reverting path repeatedly returns to a level near 0. The random walk has no such anchor and can end up anywhere, which is why a z-score is only meaningful when computed on a genuinely mean-reverting series.

body.title: The leash analogy, applied
body.scenario: You are explaining cointegration to a colleague. They say: "I don't understand how a spread between two stocks can be stationary if each stock's own price is basically a random walk that never settles down."
body.prompt: Using the leash analogy from this lesson, explain how this is possible.
body.modelAnswer: Each stock's price can wander unpredictably on its own, like a person walking without any destination, which is why individual prices are non-stationary. But if the two stocks are cointegrated, there is effectively a leash between them, a genuine economic force, such as shared business or risk-factor exposure, that keeps pulling their prices back toward a consistent relative relationship whenever they drift apart. Neither stock's price alone has to be stationary for this to work. What matters is that the specific combination of the two, the spread using the correct hedge ratio, stays bounded and keeps reverting, because the leash keeps the distance between them in check even as both wander.

cards.definition: A series where each value is the previous value plus a random shock, with no tendency to return to any fixed level. Non-stationary by definition.
A series with a stable long-run average that it consistently returns to after being pushed away by a shock. A form of stationary series.
Describes a series whose statistical properties, especially its mean, are not stable over time. Its variance typically grows the longer the series is observed.

A way of picturing cointegration: two individually wandering (non-stationary) series can still stay bounded in distance from each other if a structural force ties them together, like two people connected by a leash.

points: A stationary series has a stable mean it keeps returning to. A non-stationary series, like a random walk, has no fixed anchor and can wander indefinitely.
Individual stock prices are generally non-stationary, which is why Chapter 1 computed correlation on returns, which behave much closer to stationary.
Cointegration's genuinely surprising insight is that two individually non-stationary price series can still have a specific hedge-ratio combination, the spread, that is stationary.
The leash analogy: each stock can wander on its own, but a real economic link between them keeps the distance between their prices bounded over time.
Only a spread that behaves like the mean-reverting sample path in this lesson, not the random walk, gives a z-score real statistical meaning.
Lesson 3 introduces the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test, the standard formal test for whether a series, including a spread, is actually stationary.
